newsitem.title: USA: Coffee prices plummet, corn and lumber rise.
newsitem.headline: Coffee prices plummet, corn and lumber rise.

text.p: Coffee prices fell sharply on Monday for the second straight day as nervous speculators cashed in profits from a five-month rally.

At the Coffee Sugar and Cocoa Exchange in New York, July futures closed down 22.45 cents a pound at 253.95 cents -- down 20 percent from last Thursday's high of 318 cents, the highest price for coffee since 1977.

"The bull market is not dead, but it's got a couple of swords in its back," said Allendale Inc analyst Jim Cordier. "We may have topped out, but the fundamentals are still bullish. Coffee is still in tight supply."

Coffee stockpiles, now near 20-year lows in both consuming and producing countries, look to remain at low levels especially for high-quality "washed" arabica beans until the next Central American harvests this autumn.
Worries that cold weather could damage coffee trees in Brazil during that country's June-through-August winter season will also remain an unpredictable element in coming weeks.
"Time-wise, it's too early to call a top," said Merrill Lynch analyst Judith Ganes. "The period of tightness is only in front of us."

Analysts also said news on Friday that number two grower Colombia was offering North American roasters about 300,000 bags of green coffee for June shipment had thrown some cold water on the red-hot market.
"I think exporters in Colombia kicking out more coffee to the U.S. doesn't change the entire fundamental picture," said Cordier. "But it does alleviate some near-term tightness."
The exchange on Friday also raised margin requirements, or good faith deposits to trade each contract, in a move geared to push less well-financed traders from the market.
The charge to trade the July coffee contract rose $2,000 to $12,000 per contract.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, corn prices rose after torrential rains drenched many fields in Ohio and Indiana over the weekend and may prompt replanting of the crop.
Corn for July delivery rose 3-1/4 cents a bushel to $2.74.
"There are parts of Ohio which really got doused and that gave the market a boost. I think, though, it is a relatively small area," said Everen Securities analyst Joel Karlin.

Prices were also boosted by export demand, with U.S. exporters reporting 240,000 metric tons of corn sold to unknown foreign buyers on Monday. Net corn sales of 1,002,900 tons reported on Friday for the week ended May 22 were also well above expectations for sales of 400,000 to 500,000 tons.

At the Chicago Mercantile Exchange, lumber for July delivery closed $3 higher at $383.50 per thousand board feet after news that four British Columbia sawmills of the Canfor Corp. would take downtime later this month.
The Canfor news added to support from reports of increased demand for cash lumber at recent lower prices. But demand lacked followthrough as traders studied the reason for the Canfor closings.
"Cash has probably come up $5 or $10, but obviously they wouldn't be shutting down if business was great," said Neil Schmaedick, Smith Barney Forest Products analyst.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange, oil prices closed slightly higher in slow trading.

Crude oil for July delivery rose 10 cents to close at $20.98 a barrel, July unleaded gasoline rose 0.18 cent to end at 62.99 cents a gallon and July heating oil rose 0.48 cent to close at 56.32 cents a gallon.

On Monday, United Nations Secretary General Kofi Annan recommended extending for six months a U.N. accord that allows Iraq to sell limited amounts of oil to buy food and supplies. The deal expires on June 7.

"I think pretty much everyone expected a renewal, so there was no real surprise there," said Refco Inc analyst Victor Yu. "Gasoline season is under way and demand is good, but supply matches demand pretty well," he added.
